column2: Some, taking their sons, with most of their mounts slain, cried out; others for their fathers, others for their companions.
Kinsmen, O tiger among men, brothers and relatives some abandoned and fled here and there, O lord of men.
Many great chariot-warriors there, deeply pierced and bewildered, were seen groaning, men slain by Partha's arrows.
Others placed them on chariots, consoled them a moment, and rested, thirst relieved, they went again to battle.
Leaving them, some went again wishing to fight, doing your son's command, arrogant in battle.
Others, O best of the Bharatas, drank water, refreshed their mounts and put on armour.
Others consoled their brothers and left them in camp; some sons, others fathers; again they chose battle.
Some made ready chariots, each according to his chief, O lord of men, and leaping into the Pandava army chose battle again.
Those brave ones, covered with nets of little bells, shone like Daityas and Danavas engaged for the conquest of the three worlds.
Some suddenly came in gold-adorned chariots and fought Dhrishtadyumna in the Pandava divisions.
Dhrishtadyumna the Panchala, the great chariot-warrior Shikhandin, Nakula's son and Shatanika fought the chariot-force.
The Panchala, enraged, surrounded by a great army, rushed furiously, ready to slay yours.
As he came on, your son, O lord of men, sent many masses of arrows, O Bharata.
Then, O king, Dhrishtadyumna was swiftly struck by your son the bowman with many iron arrows in arms and chest.
Deeply pierced, the mighty archer, like an elephant with a goad, sent his four horses to death with arrows and with a broad-headed arrow took his charioteer's head from his body.
Then King Duryodhana, mounting a horse's back, tamer of foes, withdrew, his chariot slain, not far.
Seeing his own army's valour slain, your mighty son, O great king, went to where the son of Subala was.
Then, with chariots broken, three thousand great elephants surrounded the five Pandava chariot-warriors on every side.
Surrounded in the battle by the elephant force, O Bharata, those five tigers among men shone like planets covered by clouds.
Then Arjuna, O great king, having attained his aim, the mighty-armed, came out in his chariot alone, white-horsed, Krishna as charioteer.
Surrounded by mountain-like elephants on every side, he crushed the elephant-force with spotless sharp iron arrows.
We saw great elephants killed each by a single arrow, fallen and falling, split by Savyasachin.
Seeing those elephants, Bhimasena, like a rutting elephant, took a great mace in his hand, strong, and leapt from his chariot swiftly, mace in hand like Death.
Seeing the great chariot-warrior of the Pandavas with raised mace, your armies were terrified and passed dung and urine; the whole force was agitated with Vrikodara mace in hand.
We saw elephants like mountains, their temples split by Bhimasena's mace, dust-covered, running.
Those elephants, rushing, struck by Bhimasena's mace, fell crying piteously like mountains with wings cut.
Seeing those many elephants with split temples running here and there and falling, your soldiers were terrified.
Yudhishthira too, enraged, and both sons of Madri slew the elephant-fighters with vulture-feathered sharp arrows.
Dhrishtadyumna, having defeated the king in the battle, when your son had withdrawn and taken to a horse's back,
and seeing all the Pandavas surrounded by elephants, Dhrishtadyumna, O great king, with all the Prabhadrakas, the Panchala king's son, went against the elephants, wishing to kill them.
Not seeing Duryodhana, tamer of foes, in the chariot-force, Ashvatthaman, Kripa and Kritavarman the Satvata asked the kshatriyas there, "Where has Duryodhana gone?"
Not seeing the king amid the going slaughter, thinking your son slain, the great chariot-warriors, with dejected faces, asked about your son.
Some said, "Charioteer slain, he went to where Subala's son is"; others there, kshatriyas much wounded, said:
What is Duryodhana to you? You will see if he lives. Fight, all together; what will the king do for you?
Those kshatriyas, with wounded limbs, most of their mounts slain, tormented by arrows, spoke not quite clearly:
Let us kill this whole force by which we are surrounded; these Pandavas, having killed the elephants, are coming.
Hearing their words, the mighty Ashvatthaman, leaving the unbearable army of the Panchala king,
and Kripa and Kritavarman went to where Subala's son was, leaving the chariot-force, brave, firm bowmen.
Then, when they had gone, those led by Dhrishtadyumna, the Pandavas, came, O king, slaying yours.
Seeing them coming, delighted, those great chariot-warriors, valiant, your army, despairing of life, became mostly pale-faced.
Seeing them surrounded with weapons spent, O king, by a two-limbed force, giving up life,
I fought as fifth, with the Panchala's force, having stationed myself where Sharadvata (Kripa) stood.
We five fought, tormented by Kiritin's arrows, Dhrishtadyumna's great division, and a great battle took place there for us; conquered by him, we all withdrew from the battle.
Then I saw Satyaki coming, the great chariot-warrior, and the hero rushed at me in the fight with four hundred chariots.
Freed from Dhrishtadyumna with difficulty, my mount tired, I fell into the Madhava's force like a sinner into hell; there a dreadful battle took place, very terrible, for a moment.
Satyaki, the mighty-armed, destroyed my equipment and took me alive, senseless, fallen on the ground.
Then in a moment that elephant force was slain by Bhimasena's mace and Arjuna's iron arrows.
With the great elephants, mountain-like, crushed all around, the Pandavas' movement was made difficult.
Mighty Bhimasena made paths for chariots, O great king, dragging aside the great elephants of the Pandavas.
Ashvatthaman, Kripa and Kritavarman the Satvata, not seeing Duryodhana, tamer of foes, in the chariot-force, searched for the king, your mighty son,
and, leaving the Panchala, went to where Subala's son was, alarmed at not seeing the king, while the slaughter went on.
Seeing Bhimasena, tamer of foes, ranging, mace in hand like enraged Death, taker of lives,
your sons, the survivors, meeting in battle, not seeing the Kaurava Duryodhana, your son, gathered as Duryodhana's brothers and rushed at Bhimasena.
Durmarshana, Jaitra, Bhuribala and Ravi—these your sons, gathering on every side, rushed at Bhimasena and surrounded him on all sides.
Then Bhima, O great king, mounting his own chariot again, loosed sharp arrows at the vitals of your sons.
Scattered by Bhima in the great battle, your sons held Bhimasena back as one holds an elephant from a slope.
Then, enraged in the battle, Bhima swiftly crushed Durmarshana's head with a razor-arrow and felled it to the earth.
Then with another broad-headed arrow that pierces all armour, the great chariot-warrior Bhima killed your son Shrutanta.
Then piercing Jayatsena with an iron arrow, laughing as it were, the tamer of foes felled the Kaurava from his chariot seat; he fell from the chariot, O king, and died at once.
Then Shrutarva, enraged, pierced Bhima, O revered one, with a hundred straight-jointed vulture-feathered arrows.
Then, enraged in the battle, Bhima struck those three—Jaitra, Bhuribala and Ravi—with three arrows like the fire of his foes.
They fell slain to the ground from their chariots, great chariot-warriors, like kimshuka trees mottled with spring flowers cut down.
Then with another sharp iron arrow, the scorcher of foes struck Durvimochana and sent him to death.
He fell slain to the ground from his own chariot, best of chariot-warriors, like a tree on a mountain peak broken by wind.
Dushpradharsha and Sujata, your sons, he slew one by one in the battle with two arrows each at the head of the army; pierced by arrows, those two best of chariot-warriors fell.
Then, seeing another son of yours striving, Bhima pierced Durvishaha in the battle with a broad-headed arrow; he fell slain from his mount in the sight of all bowmen.
Seeing many of his brothers slain by one in the battle, Shrutarva, fallen under the power of indignation, rushed at Bhima.
Shaking a very great bow adorned with gold, loosing many arrows like poison and fire,
he, O king, cut the Pandava's bow in the great battle, and then covered him, bowless, with twenty arrows.
Then the great chariot-warrior Bhimasena, taking another bow, covered your son and said, "Stand, stand!"
A great battle took place between them, wondrous and terrible, such as of old in the battle of Jambha and Vasava.
By their arrows loosed, bright as Yama's rods, all the earth was covered, and the sky and all quarters.
Then Shrutarva, enraged, drawing his bow, struck Bhimasena in the battle with arrows in arms and chest, O king.
Deeply pierced by your son the bowman, O great king, Bhima was stirred in anger like the great ocean at the full moon.
Then Bhima, seized with rage, sent your son's charioteer and four horses to Yama's abode with arrows.
Seeing him chariotless, with feathered arrows the immeasurable-souled one covered him, showing dexterity of hand.
Shrutarva, chariotless, O king, took sword and shield; as he took them, the Pandava struck off his head from his body with a razor-arrow, and the shining sword with the hundred moons.
His head struck off, the great soul's body fell from the chariot with a resounding roar to the earth.
When that hero fell, yours, bewildered by fear, rushed in battle at Bhimasena, wishing to fight.
Armoured, the glorious Bhimasena received them as they swiftly came from the remnant of the ocean of force; they, reaching him, surrounded him on all sides.
Then, surrounded by your men with sharp arrows, Bhima tormented them all like Sahasraksha the asuras.
Then, having slain five hundred great chariot-warriors with their chariots, he again slew seven hundred of the elephant force in the battle.
Having slain ten thousand foot-soldiers with the best of arrows and eight hundred horses, the Pandava shone.
Bhimasena, son of Kunti, having slain your sons in the battle, deemed himself fulfilled, his birth fruitful, lord.
Your armies, O Bharata, did not dare to look at him as he fought and slew yours.
Having routed all the Kurus and slain their followers, he made a sound with his arms, terrifying the great elephants.
Your army, O lord of men, with most of its warriors slain, became a pitiable remnant, O great king.
Then, seeing Duryodhana stationed amid the horses, Devaki's son said to Kunti's son Dhananjaya:

The foes are mostly slain, kinsmen protected; the bull of the Shinis has turned back, having taken Sanjaya.
mahabharata:9:26.4	Nakula and Sahadeva, O Bharata, are weary, having fought the sinful followers of Dhritarashtra's son in the battle.
mahabharata:9:26.5	These three stand, having left Suyodhana: Kripa, Kritavarman and the great chariot-warrior Drona's son.
mahabharata:9:26.6	There stands the Panchala in supreme glory, having slain Duryodhana's force with all the Prabhadrakas.
mahabharata:9:26.7	There Duryodhana, Partha, stands amid the horses, looking about again and again under a held parasol.
mahabharata:9:26.8	Having arrayed the whole force, he stands in the midst of the battle; having slain him with sharp arrows you will have fulfilled your task.
mahabharata:9:26.9	Seeing the elephant force slain and you arrived, tamer of foes, slay Suyodhana before these flee.
[Arjuna said:] "Five hundred horses remain to Shakuni son of Subala, and of chariots only two hundred, Janardana; of elephants a hundred and a bit, and three thousand foot-soldiers.
Ashvatthaman, Kripa, the lord of the Trigartas, Uluka, Shakuni and Kritavarman the Satvata—
this was the remaining force of Dhritarashtra's son, Madhava; surely there is no escape from Time for anyone on earth.
With the army thus slain, see Duryodhana standing; the great king will have his foes slain by this day's end.
I think none of the enemy will escape me; those arrogant ones who do not abandon the battle today, Krishna, I shall slay them all, even if they be not human.
Today in the battle, greatly enraged, I shall end the king's long wakefulness by felling the Gandhara king with sharp arrows.
The jewels which the evil-doer Subala's son took by deceit at the dice in the assembly, I shall take them back again.
Today all the women of Nagapura will know, hearing that their husbands and sons are slain by the Pandavas in the battle.
Today all will be finished, Krishna; today Duryodhana will give up his blazing fortune and life.
If he does not flee the battle through fear, Krishna, know that foolish Dhritarashtra's son is slain.
These horses of mine cannot bear the sound of the bowstring; go on, until I slay."
Thus addressed by the glorious Pandava, the Dasharha urged the horses towards Duryodhana's force.
Seeing that division, the three ready great chariot-warriors—Bhimasena, Arjuna and Sahadeva—went with a lion-roar, wishing to kill Duryodhana.
Seeing them all together with bows raised swiftly, Subala's son rushed in battle at the Pandavas, the aggressors.
Your son Sudarshana attacked Bhimasena; Susharma and Shakuni fought Kiritin; your son, mounted on a horse, attacked Sahadeva.
Then, O lord of men, your son, without effort and quickly, struck Sahadeva hard on the head with a lance.
Struck by your son, he sat down on the chariot seat, his whole body drenched in blood, sighing like a venomous serpent.
Regaining consciousness, Sahadeva, O lord of men, enraged, covered Duryodhana with sharp arrows.
Partha, son of Kunti Dhananjaya, showing valour in the battle, cut off the heads of the brave from horses' backs.
Partha scattered that division with many arrows, felling all the horses, and went to the chariots of the Trigartas.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, gathering together, covered Arjuna and Vasudeva with showers of arrows.
Attacking Satyakarman with a razor-arrow, the greatly renowned son of Pandu then cut his chariot-pole.
With a stone-whetted razor-arrow, lord, the greatly renowned one, laughing, struck off his head adorned with heated earrings.
Then he took Satyeshu in the sight of warriors, as a hungry lion a deer in the forest, O king.
Having killed him, Partha pierced Susharma with three arrows and slew all those gold-adorned chariots.
Then Partha, hastening, loosing the keen poison of his long-stored anger, at the lord of Prasthala,
Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, filled him with a hundred arrows and then slew that bowman's horses.
Then, taking a sharp arrow like Yama's rod, he swiftly loosed it at Susharma, laughing as it were.
That arrow loosed by that bowman blazing with anger reached Susharma and split his heart in the battle.
Lifeless, O great king, he fell to the ground, gladdening all the Pandavas and pained yours.
Having slain Susharma in the battle, he sent with arrows his mighty sons—seven, eight and thirty—to destruction.
Then, having slain all his followers with sharp arrows, the great chariot-warrior went to the Bharata army, the remnant of the slain.
Bhima, enraged in the battle, O lord of men, made your son Sudarshana unseen under arrows, laughing as it were.
Then, laughing, enraged, he took off his head from his body with a very sharp razor-arrow, and he fell slain to the ground.
When that hero was slain, his followers surrounded Bhima in the battle, scattering sharp arrows.
Then Vrikodara covered that division on every side with sharp arrows touching like Indra's thunderbolt, and in a moment Bhima destroyed it, O best of the Bharatas.
While they were being destroyed, the mighty army commanders reached Bhimasena and fought, O Bharata; the Pandava covered them all with dreadful arrows.
Likewise yours, O king, surrounded the great chariot-warrior Pandavas on all sides with a great shower of arrows.
All became confused, of the Pandavas with the enemy and of yours wishing to fight the Pandavas in the battle.
Warriors fell there then, struck by one another; both armies, O king, grieved for their kinsmen.
Then, as he swiftly came, the glorious Sahadeva sent masses of arrows like swift moths, and Uluka pierced Bhima in the battle with ten arrows.
Shakuni, O great king, pierced Bhima with three arrows and covered Sahadeva with ninety arrows.
Those brave ones, O king, meeting each other in the battle, pierced one another with sharp heron-feathered gold-feathered, stone-whetted arrows loosed to the ear.
The shower of arrows from their bows loosed by their arms, O lord of men, covered all quarters like a cloud with streams.
Then, enraged in the battle, Bhima and Sahadeva, O Bharata, ranged making slaughter, the very strong ones.
Covered with hundreds of arrows by them, your force, O Bharata, became like a sky in darkness here and there.
With horses running about covered with arrows, O lord of men, a path was made here and there by dragging many slain.
With slain horses and their horsemen, with armour cut and lances split, O revered one, the earth was covered, mottled as with flowers.
The warriors there, O great king, meeting each other, ranged in the battle enraged, slaying one another.
With rolled eyes in rage and lips bitten between teeth, the earth was covered with faces with earrings like lotus filaments.
With severed arms like elephant-kings' trunks, with armlets, armour, swords, lances and axes, O great king,
with risen headless trunks cut and others dancing in the battle, the earth was filled with flocks of flesh-eaters, dreadful, O lord.
When the force of the Kauravas was reduced to a remnant in the great battle, the Pandavas, delighted, sent them to Yama's abode.
In the meantime the brave and glorious son of Subala struck Sahadeva hard on the head with a lance; he sat bewildered on the chariot seat, O great king.
Seeing Sahadeva so, the glorious Bhimasena, enraged, held back all the armies, O Bharata.
He pierced them with iron arrows by hundreds and thousands, and, having pierced them, uttered a lion-roar, tamer of foes.
Terrified by that sound, all with horses and elephants suddenly fled in fear, and the followers of Shakuni.
Seeing them broken, King Duryodhana said, "Turn back, you who do not know dharma! Fight; what is flight to you?
Having established fame here, one gains the worlds hereafter; the hero who gives up life in the battle without showing his back..."
Thus addressed by the king, the followers of Subala's son advanced on the Pandavas, making death their return.
A very dreadful sound was made by those rushing, O king of kings, like the agitated ocean, agitated on every side.
Seeing the followers of Subala's son rush, the Pandavas, intent on victory, met them, O great king.
Recovered, the unconquerable Sahadeva, O lord of men, pierced Shakuni with ten arrows and his horses with three, and, laughing as it were, cut the bow of Subala's son with arrows.
Then, taking another bow, Shakuni, arrogant in battle, pierced Nakula with sixty and Bhimasena with seven.
Uluka too, O great king, pierced Bhima with seven and Sahadeva with seventy, wishing to save his father in the battle.
Bhimasena in the battle pierced him with sharp arrows, Shakuni with sixty-four, and those at the sides with three each.
Struck by Bhima with oil-sharpened iron arrows, they, enraged, covered Sahadeva in the battle with showers of arrows, as clouds with lightning cover a mountain with streams of water.
Then the brave, glorious Sahadeva, as Uluka came on, O great king, took off his head with a broad-headed arrow.
He went from his chariot to the earth, felled by Sahadeva, his whole body drenched in blood, gladdening the Pandavas in the battle.
Seeing his son slain, Shakuni there, O Bharata, with tear-choked throat, sighing and remembering Kshatta's words,
reflected a moment, his eyes full of tears and sighing, reached Sahadeva and pierced him with three arrows.
Warding off the arrows loosed with masses of arrows, the glorious Sahadeva, O great king, cut his bow in the battle.
With his bow cut, O king of kings, Shakuni son of Subala then took a great sword and hurled it at Sahadeva.
As it suddenly came, dreadful, O lord of men, he cut it in two, laughing as it were, in the battle.
Seeing the sword cut in two, he took a great mace and hurled it at Sahadeva; it fell vain on the ground.
Looking at the forest region frequented by creatures of many kinds, he, the mighty-armed, saw a banyan tree with a multitude of crows.
Your sons fell into that kindled fire like moths; they were burned by Keshava's flame; you ought not to grieve.
His mother, greedy for sons, again said to her son, "Do good to the brothers whose good you wish."
I am guilty and to be killed, and you, serpent, are guilty; for you yourself name yourself the cause here, serpent.
To him speaking thus, Vyasa, knower of dharma, of great splendour, then spoke consoling, auspicious and meaningful words.
And Dhritarashtra looked on those heroes, trained and established in discipline, always like pupils, as on a teacher.
Asses were born among cows, mules among camels and she-mules; cats among dogs and mice among mongooses.
Yudhishthira, mighty-armed; Bhimasena, scorcher of foes; Arjuna and the two heroes, the sons of the Ashvins—listen to my word.
And Bhima of terrible valour, dearer to me than life, and Arjuna like Indra, and the two twins like Yama—
